Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis. Core Radiology liver coverage was reviewed for HCC, adenoma, cystic liver disease, metastases, and liver trauma; RadPrimer supplies the differential hierarchy and shared article backbone; STATdx supplies the selected 23-image teaching library and additional case detail.

  • Hemorrhagic hepatic cyst: clot may mimic a solid tumor, but blood products do not enhance; ultrasound may show organizing hematoma/fibrin strands and MRI signal depends on the blood stage.
  • ADPLD: innumerable nonenhancing simple cysts may be present; on T1 MRI, simple-fluid cysts are dark while hemorrhagic cysts can be bright.

  • Less common: coagulopathic hepatic hemorrhage, hepatic metastases, HELLP syndrome, and amyloidosis.
🧪 Modality Pivots
  • Core HCC: classic CT/MRI pattern is arterial enhancement with portal venous washout and an enhancing capsule; HCC can be slightly T2 hyperintense and may restrict diffusion.

column11: How does the cirrhotic nodule-to-HCC pathway explain the shift toward arterial-phase hyperenhancement?
column12: Core describes progression in cirrhosis from regenerative nodule -> dysplastic nodule -> HCC. Regenerative nodules are portal-vein supplied and should not arterially enhance; most dysplastic nodules also remain predominantly portal supplied, although high-grade dysplastic nodules can begin to enhance arterially. HCC develops neovascularity and the classic phenotype becomes arterial hyperenhancement with portal venous/delayed washout and capsule. Radiology pivot: increasing arterialization within the cirrhotic nodule pathway moves the lesion toward HCC, while regenerative/low-grade dysplastic nodules usually lack the full pattern.

column11: Why does hepatic adenoma usually show little HIDA uptake and often appear photopenic on sulfur-colloid scintigraphy?
column12: Core describes hepatic adenoma as hepatocytes with scattered Kupffer cells but no bile ducts. The absence of biliary ductules explains the paucity of HIDA uptake. Sulfur-colloid uptake depends on reticuloendothelial/Kupffer-cell activity, so adenomas are usually photopenic, although Core notes this is not absolute. Radiology pivot: FNH contains bile ductules and more functional Kupffer-cell architecture, so HIDA/sulfur-colloid behavior can help separate FNH from adenoma.

column13: What pitfall can make a hemorrhagic hepatic cyst look like a solid tumor, and what safety check prevents the error?
column14:
Trap: Mistaking clotted intracystic blood for an enhancing mural tumor.
Safety check: Assess enhancement on pre- and postcontrast imaging.
Discriminator: The article states that clotted blood in a hepatic cyst may mimic tumor but will not enhance.
Why it happens: Hemorrhage increases internal attenuation/complexity and can simulate soft tissue.

column15: On CT, what imaging findings define the AAST liver injury grades I-V in Core Radiology?
column16:
Grade I: subcapsular hematoma <10% surface or laceration <1 cm.
Grade II: subcapsular hematoma 10-50%, intraparenchymal hematoma <10 cm, or laceration 1-3 cm.
Grade III: subcapsular hematoma >50%, ruptured hematoma, laceration >3 cm, or contained vascular injury/active bleeding.

Grade V: >75% lobar destruction or retrohepatic IVC/central hepatic vein injury.
Exam pivot: Grade the highest imaging injury; multiple injuries advance one grade up to grade III.

column15: When a hemorrhagic hepatic mass is hypervascular, what source-supported clues favor adenoma versus HCC?

Adenoma: hemorrhage is common; spontaneous bleeding in/around a mass in a young woman without cirrhosis is almost diagnostic; fat, multiplicity, and encapsulation may be present.
